name: diStorm3
baseline: Capstone, Zydis, Intel XED, bddisasm, udis86 and BeaEngine (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB .text section of Firefox 86.0.1's 64-bit xul.dll, throughput in MB/s (computed as bytes/1024/1024 per second). The README does not state the loop count: bench.py's built-in default is 20 passes over the 36.4 MiB section of the older 63 MB input/xul.dll checked into the repo, and with a custom file and no loop-count argument it scales the count to keep the same total bytes (about 9 passes over a 77 MB section, derived from bench.py). The Firefox 86 xul.dll itself is not in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Decode plus format: 58.85 MB/s versus Zydis 22.24, bddisasm 16.00, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02, BeaEngine 13.42, udis86 12.02 MB/s (about 4.2x Capstone, derived from page data); second only to iced (149.21). Decode only: 92.17 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, bddisasm 35.48, Zydis 34.19, udis86 80.72 MB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1 (disas-bench README). make-all.sh builds the C libraries with gcc and LTO: Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, XED via mfile.py --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto, diStorm via its own make/linux Makefile (current version: -fPIC -O2 -std=c99) with -flto prepended, BeaEngine patched to -O3 -flto, udis86 without LTO (it got slower). The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. C libraries and yaxpeax-x86 are pinned git submodules (last updated March 2021); iced is pulled unpinned from its git master at build time.
tradeoffs: Plain C with a single API (about 45 KB per its README), callable directly from C++. Decodes x86/AMD64 only; coverage of recent instruction-set extensions was not checked.
caveats: Numbers are from the iced author's disas-bench fork (June 2021, i5-6600K) with the diStorm submodule of March 2021; diStorm's last commit is 2021-12-18 (v3.5.3), so it is abandoned and instruction-set coverage added since then by other decoders was not checked. The diStorm README itself gives no numbers, only 'ultra fast' and a 2014 thesis quote ('chose diStorm3, which had the best performance'). The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode+format driver discards distorm_format64's output, but its time is well above decode-only (58.85 vs 92.17 MB/s), so formatting work is being timed. Formatters differ in output syntax between libraries. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart without numbers) shows diStorm at roughly 138 MB/s decode and 86 MB/s decode+format, still ahead of Capstone, XED, Zydis and bddisasm but behind iced and yaxpeax (values read off the bars, approximate). The comparison is decode/disassembly throughput against other disassembler libraries, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump/libopcodes was not tested.

name: iced (iced-x86)
baseline: Capstone, Zydis and Intel XED (other x86/x86-64 disassembler libraries; objdump was not tested)
workload: Decoding only, and decoding plus formatting, of the 77 MB .text section of Firefox 86.0.1's 64-bit xul.dll, throughput in MB/s (computed as bytes/1024/1024 per second). The Firefox 86 xul.dll itself is not in the repo.
claimed_speedup: Decode only: 256.69 MB/s versus XED 55.39, Zydis (min) 61.33, Zydis 34.19, bddisasm 35.48, diStorm 92.17 MB/s. Decode plus format: 149.21 MB/s versus diStorm 58.85, Zydis 22.24, XED 15.67, Capstone 14.02 MB/s (about 10.6x Capstone, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Kubuntu 21.04, gcc 10.3.0, Rust 1.52.1 (disas-bench README). make-all.sh builds the C libraries with gcc and LTO: Capstone and bddisasm as CMake Release builds with CFLAGS=-flto, XED via mfile.py --opt=3 --extra-flags=-flto, diStorm via its own make/linux Makefile (current version: -fPIC -O2 -std=c99) with -flto prepended, BeaEngine patched to -O3 -flto, udis86 without LTO (it got slower). The C bench drivers (bench/*/Makefile) are built with -flto -O3; the Zydis driver is a CMake Release build with CFLAGS=-flto. The Rust drivers (bench/iced-x86/Cargo.toml, bench/yaxpeax/Cargo.toml) use a release profile with opt-level=3, lto=true, codegen-units=1 and no target-cpu setting. C libraries and yaxpeax-x86 are pinned git submodules (last updated March 2021); iced is pulled unpinned from its git master at build time.
tradeoffs: Rust crate (bindings for .NET, Java, Python, Lua, JavaScript via WebAssembly per its README); no C or C++ API in the repo, so C++ projects need FFI. Decoded instruction is 40 bytes and the decoder allocates nothing. Also contains an encoder and a code assembler.
caveats: First-party run: disas-bench is a fork of athre0z/disas-bench (MIT, Joel Höner 2017) hosted in iced's own organisation, and the June 2021 results were committed by the iced author; the iced driver's Cargo.toml was written by the yaxpeax author. iced is pulled unpinned from git master at build time, so the measured version is whatever master was in June 2021. The benchmark loop count is not stated (see workload). Each driver runs once per configuration (no repetitions or variance); the C drivers time CPU time with clock(), the Rust drivers wall time with millisecond resolution. The decode-only driver never reads the decoded Instruction (only the decoder position advances), so LTO could drop some operand stores. The decode+format driver uses iced's SpecializedFormatter from the fast_fmt feature with db/dw/dd/dq output disabled and the output-buffer check turned off, the cheapest formatter iced offers, while the C libraries use their general formatters; formatted text differs between libraries. Capstone and BeaEngine have no decode-only mode. The yaxpeax author's later fork (i7-12700K, GCC 11, rustc 1.67 nightly, bar chart only) shows iced at roughly 357 MB/s decode and 217 MB/s decode+format, with yaxpeax-x86 about level on decode (values read off the bars). iced has no C or C++ API (it ships Rust, .NET, Java, Python, JavaScript/WebAssembly and Lua bindings), so C++ users need their own FFI shim. The five newest commits (2026-07-14) are dependabot dependency bumps. Decode/disassembly throughput against other disassemblers, not assembly speed against GNU as, NASM or MASM (the category's spec baseline); objdump was not tested.

name: STOKE
baseline: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 compiled x86-64 code (output quality); expert hand-written assembly for some kernels; Google Native Client's shipped libc string functions in the 2017 paper
workload: Runtime of superoptimized loop-free x86-64 kernels (OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication, Hacker's Delight, SAXPY, linked-list traversal) starting from llvm -O0 code, and 13 libc string functions from NaCl newlib.
claimed_speedup: ASPLOS 2013 paper, Figure 1 caption and Section 1: the OpenSSL big-number Montgomery multiplication kernel rewritten by STOKE is '16 lines shorter, 1.6x faster' than the gcc -O3 code 'and slightly faster than expert handwritten assembly'. Abstract: STOKE's programs 'either match or outperform the code produced by gcc -O3, icc -O3, and in some cases, expert handwritten assembly'. Figure 11 plots speedups over llvm -O0 for Hacker's Delight p01-p25, saxpy, mont and list; per-kernel values appear only in the chart. The README's popcount tutorial times a loop at 1.046 s for g++ -O3 -fno-inline versus 0.133 s after STOKE patches popcnt() (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 and icc -O3 baselines (versions not stated in the extracted paper text); gcc-4.9 used in the 2017 paper's translation mode; README tutorial uses g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -fno-inline
hardware: ASPLOS 2013: synthesis and optimization on a cluster of 40 dual-core 1.8 GHz AMD Opterons (machine used for the runtime speedups not identified in the extracted text); ASPLOS 2017: machines with two Intel Xeon E5-2667v2 3.3 GHz processors and 256 GB RAM
tradeoffs: x86-64 only and Intel-microarchitecture oriented. Needs test cases plus bounded or SMT-based equivalence checking, search budgets of tens of minutes per kernel on a cluster, and works best on short loop-free sequences. README: 'STOKE isn't production ready' and 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it says it is 'not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code'.
caveats: The paper is from 2013 and the speedups are on a small set of hand-picked loop-free kernels, plotted relative to llvm -O0 starting points in Figure 11; per-kernel numbers are chart-only, and the paper states no gcc/icc versions and does not name the timing machine. The README says 'We're not quite at the point where we can take a generic loop and expect to improve gcc/llvm -O3 code', calls STOKE a research prototype that 'isn't production ready', and says 'nobody is actively working on this code base'; it needs gcc 4.9 to build. The README popcount tutorial's ~8x win compares against g++ -O3 without -march, so gcc cannot emit the popcnt instruction that STOKE uses; it shows the tool working, not a fair compiler comparison. The category fit (assembly tooling) is a judgement call: STOKE is a superoptimizer, and its baselines are compilers, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. The last commit (2020-12-04) only added a CodeQL workflow; the last code change is from 2019-10-03.

name: aron
baseline: macOS as (the system assembler on macOS, not GNU as)
workload: Assembling the repo's test.macos.s, a 31-line clang -S (Intel syntax) output of a hello-world printf program, once per process, with aron versus the macOS assembler; timings are dominated by process startup.
claimed_speedup: README screenshot (imgs/aron-bm.png) of 'hyperfine -N --warmup 10 "target/release/aron test.macos.s" "as test.macos.s"': aron 3.9 ms +/- 0.7 ms (777 runs) versus as 49.8 ms +/- 2.3 ms (60 runs), summary 'aron ... ran 12.94 +/- 2.34 times faster than as'. The README introduces it with 'This is not empirical by any means'.
compiler_and_flags: aron built with cargo release profile (target/release); the screenshot's shell prompt shows rust v1.60.0 and C v13.1.6-clang (Apple clang 13.1.6 toolchain, which supplies the baseline as), aron v0.1.0; timed with hyperfine -N --warmup 10. No other flags stated.
hardware: A macOS machine; CPU model not stated.
tradeoffs: Incomplete x86-64 assembler (README says so); outputs ELF and Mach-O objects; supports only part of the instruction set and directives, so it cannot replace GNU as, NASM or MASM on general input.
caveats: The README says 'This is not empirical by any means'. One 31-line hello-world input (about 15 instructions), so both timings measure process launch rather than assembly: aron finishes in 3.9 ms while macOS as, a driver that hands off to clang's integrated assembler, takes 49.8 ms mostly in startup. No CPU is named, the output objects are not compared, and the assembler is self-described as incomplete, so the speedup also reflects its narrower feature set. The baseline is macOS as, not GNU as. The screenshot was taken on aron v0.1.0 (August 2022); the repo is now at 0.2.0. The language is Rust (Cargo.toml, edition 2021) although the repo page shows no language bar.

name: MaxAs
baseline: cuBLAS sgemm (NVIDIA's library kernels, compiled by NVIDIA's toolchain)
workload: Hand-scheduled single-precision GEMM kernels written in Maxwell SASS and assembled with MaxAs, versus cuBLAS sgemm, on large (4096) and small matrices.
claimed_speedup: SGEMM walkthrough: 'performing as much as 25% over cublas' for small matrices (64-thread version) and 'beating cublas by 4.8%' at size 4096 (256-thread version); about 98% of theoretical peak on GM107 and 96% on GM204. Absolute GFLOPS appear only in chart images.
hardware: NVIDIA GM204 (Maxwell) at a sustained 1607 MHz core clock (1620 MHz boost scores excluded) with 8000 MHz memory; GM107 also cited for the 98% efficiency figure. Card model, driver, CUDA and cuBLAS versions are not stated on the page.
tradeoffs: Assembler for NVIDIA Maxwell SASS only (GTX 9xx era), written in Perl; the repository is archived and Intel has discontinued the project. Gains come from hand-written kernels and scheduling, not from the assembler alone.
caveats: First-party wiki claim; exact per-size GFLOPS are only in chart images, and the page names no cuBLAS, CUDA or driver version, no card model and no flags. The public harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp with sgemm.pl, a Windows Visual Studio build) has its cuBLAS timing code commented out, so the comparison cannot be rerun as published. The author says the kernels were 'derived from detailed study of the cublas Kepler and Maxwell sgemm implementations', and part of the gap comes from a cuBLAS bug that the wiki says costs cuBLAS sgemm 28 GFLOPS on GM204; the 2015-era cuBLAS has long since been superseded. The speedup is of a hand-scheduled SASS kernel against a library, not of the assembler against ptxas, GNU as, NASM or MASM; MaxAs only targets Maxwell (later partial half and dp4a support). Archived by the owner on 2023-01-03 with an Intel discontinuation notice; the last code commit is from 2016-06-10. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.

The harness (sgemm/sgemm.cpp, sgemm.pl) is public but its cuBLAS timing calls are commented out, it builds as a Windows Visual Studio project, and no CUDA, cuBLAS or driver version or card model is given, so not A; no independent head-to-head found (maxDNN arXiv 1501.06633 reports 96% efficiency for a maxas-style SGEMM, snippet only, no cuBLAS comparison).
verification.notes: Wiki numbers match the record (25% small-matrix, 4.8% at 4096, 98%/96% efficiency). Shortcomings: first-party, GFLOPS chart-only, no cuBLAS/CUDA versions or card model, cuBLAS comparison code commented out in the published harness, kernels derived from cuBLAS's own SASS plus a cuBLAS bug, archived 2023 (last code 2016).

The speedup is of a hand-written kernel against a 2015-era library, not of the assembler against GNU as, NASM or MASM. Treat as a reference, not a general assembler win.

name: SuperCoder
workload: Runtime speedup of LLM-rewritten x86 assembly versus the gcc -O3 assembly on a benchmark of 8,072 real-world programs averaging 130 lines (CodeNet-derived), with test-based correctness checks.
claimed_speedup: Per WebSearch result text of arXiv 2505.11480 only (paper not opened): the RL-fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct model reaches a 95.0% test pass rate and a 1.46x average speedup over gcc -O3; the strongest baseline LLM (Claude-opus-4) reaches 51.5% pass rate and 1.43x average speedup.
compiler_and_flags: gcc -O3 baseline stated in search-result text; flags and timing harness (hyperfine) not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Probabilistic output: correctness is test-based (95.0% pass rate, not formal equivalence), so rewrites need independent verification. Needs a GPU-capable RL setup (verl) to retrain; model weights and dataset are listed on Hugging Face in the README.
caveats: Numbers come from search-result text only; the repo README has no results section and states no hardware or compiler flags. Averages are over test-passing programs as reported by the authors, so failed rewrites are excluded from the speedup mean (not verified on the paper). Preprint status; 2 commits in the repo.

name: Fadec
baseline: libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis (x86 decoding libraries)
workload: Decoding x86-32 and x86-64 instructions with a lookup-table decoder; a separate x86-64 encoder is included.
claimed_speedup: 'Fadec is significantly faster than libopcodes, Capstone, or Zydis due to the absence of high-level abstractions and the small lookup table' (no numbers); encoder API v2 'about 3x faster than v1' (internal comparison).
stars_or_usage: 235 stars, 33 forks, 432 commits (github.com page, 2026-10-11). Used as a git submodule (deps/fadec) by the TPDE compiler back-end framework (tpde2/tpde .gitmodules, opened). Search results also show copies at android.googlesource.com platform/external/lfi/fadec (tagged android-17.0.0_r1) and a Chromium mirror chromium.googlesource.com/external/github.com/aengelke/fadec, plus forks oleavr/fadec and GenKyoko/fadec (snippet only; googlesource host did not resolve here).
tradeoffs: C library with no dependencies, about 95 KiB with decoder and encoder, usable in freestanding environments. Targets Intel 64 behaviour; AMD-specific differences are not handled. Decoded operand sizes are not always exact for speed.
caveats: No benchmark numbers or comparison harness anywhere: the speed claim over libopcodes, Capstone and Zydis is qualitative, and the only timing tool in the repo (decode-profile.c, added 2026-06-01) measures Fadec alone. Fadec is absent from the public disas-bench candidate lists (athre0z and iximeow forks). The encoder v2 '3x faster than v1' figure is an internal comparison with no baseline and comes at ~3 MiB code size (off by default, -Dwith_encode2=true). README lists known issues: low test coverage, register-uniqueness constraints not enforced (VSIB, AMX, AVX-512 FP16 complex multiply), decoded operand sizes not always exact, AMD64-specific behaviour not handled (Intel 64 semantics only), MPX, HLE, XOP, FMA4 and Xeon Phi unsupported. Baselines are disassembler libraries, not GNU as, NASM or MASM. Notability rests on reuse (TPDE, Android LFI, Chromium mirror) rather than stars. Canonical CI pulls from git.sr.ht/~aengelke/fadec.

name: SLOTHY
baseline: unscheduled 'clean' hand-written assembly and prior hand-optimized implementations of the same kernels (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs, FFT, X25519); no compiler baseline stated on the pages opened
workload: Instruction scheduling, register allocation and software pipelining of hand-written Arm AArch64, Armv8.1-M and RISC-V assembly for cryptographic and DSP kernels.
claimed_speedup: README: SLOTHY has been used 'to provide the fastest known implementations of various cryptographic and DSP primitives' (ML-KEM and ML-DSA NTTs for Cortex-A55/A72/M55/M85, FFT for Cortex-M55/M85, X25519 for Cortex-A55); no speedup numbers on any page opened. Related adoption number: the AWS-LC pull request that imported the s2n-bignum X25519 rewrite (partly SLOTHY-generated) reports 12867.1 to 22361.9 ops/sec ('74% speedup') on Graviton 2, but that gain is not attributable to SLOTHY alone.
hardware: Targets Cortex-M55, M85, A55 (supported), A72, Cortex-X/Neoverse-V, Apple M1 (experimental) and XuanTie C908
stars_or_usage: 352 stars; adopted in AWS-LC / s2n-bignum, Arm EndpointAI CMSIS DSP and mlkem-native
tradeoffs: Microarchitecture-specific by design: each output is scheduled for one core model (portability note: code tuned for Cortex-A55 is not tuned for other cores). Solver time is seconds to minutes for under 50 instructions and minutes to hours for up to 150 instructions; larger kernels need heuristics. Python tool using Google OR-Tools.
caveats: The paper (CHES 2024, eprint 2022/1303) and its numbers could not be opened (eprint.iacr.org blocked), so no measured speedup is confirmed. The repo ships the clean and optimized sources and a reproduction artifact (paper/, paper/artifact) but cycle benchmarks need physical boards and were not run or read. The AWS-LC PR (#1469) was closed unmerged and mixes an algorithm change with SLOTHY scheduling.
found_via: github.com/topics/superoptimization (WebFetch); opened the slothy README, paper/README.md, LICENSE and AWS-LC / s2n-bignum PR pages
